Don Tiare And His Orchestra Exotique

  "The Music Of Les Baxter"




····

a merger of the talents
of two geniuses
of the
sensuous
and exotic
····
The bamboo-covered skiff bobbing its businesslike way to shore in Sampan Landing, the lush overhanging greenery of Jungle Trails, the peaceful dialog of earth and wind in Quiet Village, the capricious freedom of the Cockatoo, and the nocturnal creature noises of Crickets of Karachi -- these and kindred commonplaces of other hemispheres inspire the palette of Les Baxter's musical impressionism.
And if it may be said that Baxter paints pictures with sound, it is no conceit to add that Don Tiare gives us the three-dimensional "sight" to hear them with.
This is an album that merges the talents of two geniuses of the sensuous and exotic -- one, the composer of richly-textured mood pieces that hint of an underlying mystery in the primitive world; the other, a renowned interpretive artist whose "orchestra exotique" makes a pulsating specialty of the rare tone colors that are called for.
Don Tiare is an international performer whose expressive combo is as familiar in Bangkok as in Bordeaux, as comfortable in Nikko as in Nice, and as suited to the dinner jacket of the London Savoy as to the pareu on the beaches of Tahiti. Long an admirer of the unique Les Baxter creations, he asked the composer to write some original pieces for this album; and those, along with such Baxter standards as Quiet Village, Bangkok Cockfight and Crickets of Karachi, make up a dazzling and somewhat intoxicating tour of the far away places.
Tiare and Baxter together work a spell upon all the senses, so that listening becomes more than an experience of sound and sight but one that keeps the imagination astir with notions of taste and feeling, with tropical heat and pungent aromas. Above all, there is a sense of movement that runs through each of these compositions, whether the motion be that of cruising breezes, rolling waters, the staccato of animal combat, or the vivacity of the Girl Behind the Bamboo Curtain and the quickened pulse of the beholder.
Those of us who have never been privileged to witness the spectacle of the sun coming up in Hong Kong -- who have never known the romance of nightfall in a Pakistani seaport, nor listened to the trees in a Polynesian village, nor been party to the gaiety of a Thailand festival -- will be enriched by what unfolds here.
And for all that, this is music that is marvelously danceable -- in fact, compellingly so.
(album notes)

German pianist, composer, conductor, arranger, producer and music publisher. Born on March 11th 1926 in Nuremberg, Germany, died on December 27th, 2003 in Starnberg, Germany. Heinz Kiessling (March 11, 1926 – December 27, 2003) was a German musician, conductor, composer, and music producer, known mainly from his work for popular films and television programs. Kiessling's piece Temptation Sensation (originally titled Haute Couture) is the theme song for It's Always Sunny in Philadelphia, the longest-running live-action sitcom in American television history. The series also uses background music during its episodes from Kiessling, including On your Bike and Blue Blood (originally titled Tandem-Holiday and Pizzicata Milanese respectively).
Life and career: Kiessling studied piano, composition, and conducting after World War II at the Nuremberg Conservatory in 1949, and started his career in 1949 as a pianist and played in different concerts around the world. Soon after, he started working on recording music for television. In 1950, he began composing music in the jazz, dance, and light music genres. At times, he also led his own orchestra, and also worked many years for the RIAS Big Band [de] in Berlin. Together with the pianist Werner Tautz, he established in 1964 the label "Brilliant" through which he managed numerous national and international big bands.
Kiessling worked with many national and international stars, including Chet Baker, Luis Bonfa, Wenche Myhre, and Caterina Valente. For over two decades, he accompanied the shows of Peter Alexander. In addition, Kiessling composed the songs and scene music for numerous films and television productions, including Klimbim [de], Zwei himmlische Töchter, Dingsda [de], Das Traumschiff and Aktenzeichen XY... ungelöst. In total he produced over 1200 tunes and also published some of his own recordings which made him become one of the most successful German "easy listening" composers of the post-war period.
Notable works: In 1969, Kiessling wrote "In the Shadow of the Moon" for Reprise, which later on became the theme song for Frank Sinatra's daughter Tina Sinatra TV mini-series Romeo und Julia '70. ... His piece "Temptation Sensation" is used as the theme song for the FX and FXX TV show It's Always Sunny in Philadelphia. ... Many of Kiessling's other orchestral production music compositions are featured on the show such as "Hotsy-Totsy" and "Honey Bunch". ... -- Wikipedia

John Towner Williams and Co.

     "World On A String: Music of Harold Arlen" 


  ····   


WORLD ON A STRING
BY
JOHN TOWNER WILLIAMS
   ····   
As in the case of so many other highly skilled musicians, John Towner Williams chose not to take the night club glory-road to fame, but decided to accept the comparative obscurity but far greater security that is the lot of a Hollywood "studio" musician. Perhaps his marriage to beautiful Hollywood actress Barbara Ruick helped to influence his decision. But no matter what the reasons, he is a musician with something to say one who should be heard. For this reason, Bethlehem Records is proud to present John's introductory album, World On A String.
Although still young (he was born in 1932 in Flushing, New York), John Williams has covered considerable mileage in the music world. It is highly possible that
because of his father, being a professional musician he decided on music as a career. After early training in the East, he moved to Los Angeles, where he studied under Robert Van Eps. After a hitch in the Air Force, he returned to civilian life in 1955 to start his professional musical career in earnest. He quickly earned an impressive string of credits, which included working as a pianist for the Broadway musical production of Three For Tonight, and accompanying the conducting for both Howard Keel and Vic Damone. A classical background, as well as an impressive jazz feeling account for his popularity as both an arranger and pianist in West Coast musical circles. As a pianist, he now works for some of Hollywood's finest conductors  —  names such as Les Baxter, Jerry Fielding, Frank de Vol,
Nelson Riddle and Leith Stevens. As an arranger, his credits include albums for Yvonne De Carlo, Dick Stabile, musical numbers for the Marge and Gower Champion television series and arrangements for many well known jazz groups.
For this debut album, John has showcased the best tunes from the folio of one of the most prolific and talented of contemporary song writers, Harold Arlen. The tunes selected are familiar to all, and are treated in a manner which is fresh and imaginative. Unlike many musicians with jazz leanings, he has the ability to arrange and play a selection with true jazz feeling, yet present it in a manner understandable to all. He does not take away from, but adds to the feeling and mood of these numbers with his imaginative interpretations.
This is a "finger-snappin'" album, with a swinging but never obtrusive beat. For maximum contrast, John used three different musical combinations: five trombones and three rhythm instruments, four saxophones and three rhythm and two saxophones with two trumpets and three rhythm. The musicians included in the groups were hand-selected, and among the best in the field. The music performed here is further evidence of their ability. It is hard to pick favorites from among the twelve selections included on this album, since all are of consistently high musical caliber, but mention should be made of Herb Geller's sax solos on both Old Black Magic and Over the Rainbow, Milt Bernhart's trombone on The Devil and the Deep Blue Sea, Gene Cipriano's relaxed and swinging sax chorus on World on a String and Francis Howard's moody trombone passage on Stormy Weather. ... and once you've listened, we feel you'll join us in a big hand for
John Towner Williams pianist, arranger and leader.
    (album notes) 


-------
   John Towner Williams (born February 8, 1932)  is an American composer and conductor. Over his seven-decade career, he has composed many of the best known scores in film history. His compositional style blends romanticism, impressionism, and atonal music with complex orchestration.  Best known for his collaborations with George Lucas and Steven Spielberg, he has received numerous accolades, including 27 Grammy Awards, ...  . With a total of 54 Academy Award nominations, he is the second-most nominated person in the award's history, after Walt Disney. ...

Williams's early work as a film composer includes None but the Brave (1965), Valley of the Dolls (1967), Goodbye, Mr. Chips (1969),  ... and The Towering Inferno (1974). He has collaborated with Spielberg since The Sugarland Express (1974), composing music for all but five of his feature films. He received five Academy Awards for Best Score/Best Score Adaptation for Fiddler on the Roof (1971; score adaptation of the original music by Jerry Bock), Jaws (1975), Star Wars (1977), E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial (1982) and Schindler's List (1993). Other memorable collaborations with Spielberg include Close Encounters of the Third Kind (1977), the Indiana Jones franchise (1981–2023), Hook (1991), Jurassic Park (1993) and its sequel The Lost World: Jurassic Park (1997), Saving Private Ryan (1998), Catch Me If You Can (2002), War Horse (2011), Lincoln (2012), and The Fabelmans (2022). He also scored Superman (1978),  ...

Outside of his long-term collaborations with Spielberg and Lucas, Williams has composed the scores for films directed by William Wyler, Clint Eastwood, Alfred Hitchcock, Brian De Palma, John Badham, George Miller, Oliver Stone, Chris Columbus, Ron Howard, Barry Levinson, John Singleton,  ...  . He has also composed numerous classical concertos and other works for orchestral ensembles and solo instruments.  ... Other works by Williams include theme music for the 1984 Summer Olympic Games; NBC Sunday Night Football; "The Mission" theme (used by NBC News and Seven News in Australia); PBS's Great Performances and the television series Lost in Space, Land of the Giants and Amazing Stories. 

Williams received the Kennedy Center Honor in 2004,  ... He has composed the scores for nine of the top 25 highest-grossing films at the U.S. box office. In 2022, Williams was awarded an honorary knighthood by Queen Elizabeth II, "for services to film music". In 2005, the American Film Institute placed Williams' score to Star Wars first on its list AFI's 100 Years of Film Scores; his scores for Jaws and E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial also made the list. The Library of Congress entered the Star Wars soundtrack into the National Recording Registry for being "culturally, historically, or aesthetically significant". 

Early life and education:  Following his studies at the Juilliard School of Music and the Eastman School of Music, Williams moved back to Los Angeles, where he began working as an orchestrator at film studios. During this period, Williams worked with such composers as Franz Waxman, Bernard Herrmann and Alfred Newman, and with fellow orchestrators Conrad Salinger and Bob Franklyn. 

Williams was also a studio pianist and session musician, performing scores by Jerry Goldsmith, Elmer Bernstein and Henry Mancini. One of his first jobs was working under mentor Alfred Newman with an uncredited orchestral role for Carousel (1956), which coincidentally starred his soon-to-be wife Barbara Ruick. 

With Mancini, he recorded the scores of Peter Gunn (1959), Breakfast at Tiffany's (1961), Days of Wine and Roses (1962) and Charade (1963), and played the piano part of the guitar-piano ostinato in Mancini's Peter Gunn title theme. With Elmer Bernstein, he performed the scores for Alexander Mackendrick's Sweet Smell of Success (1957) and Robert Mulligan's To Kill a Mockingbird (1962). Williams was also the pianist of Billy Wilder's The Apartment (1960), Jerome Robbins and Robert Wise's West Side Story (1961) and Blake Edwards's The Great Race (1966). 

He released several jazz albums under the name Johnny Williams, including Jazz Beginnings, World on a String and The John Towner Touch.  Williams also served as music arranger and bandleader for a series of popular music albums alongside Ray Vasquez and Frankie Laine.       ...    --  Wikipedia

  Leslie Thompson Baxter (March 14, 1922 – January 15, 1996) was an American composer, conductor, and musician. After working as an arranger and composer for swing bands, he developed his own style of easy listening music, known as exotica, and scored over 250 radio, television and motion pictures numbers. 

Baxter studied piano at the Detroit Conservatory of Music before moving to Los Angeles for further studies at Pepperdine College. From 1943 on he played tenor and baritone saxophone for the Freddie Slack big band. Abandoning a concert career as a pianist, he turned to popular music as a singer. At the age of 23 he joined Mel Tormé's Mel-Tones, singing on Artie Shaw records such as "What Is This Thing Called Love?" 

Baxter then turned to arranging and conducting for Capitol Records in 1950 and conducted the orchestra in two early Nat King Cole hits, "Mona Lisa" and "Too Young". He also recorded Yma Sumac's first album: Voice of the Xtabay, which can be considered one of the first recordings of exotica. In 1951, he made the original recording of "Quiet Village", which years later became a hit for Martin Denny. In 1953, he scored his first movie, the sailing travelogue Tanga Tika. 

With his own orchestra, he released a number of hits, including "Ruby" (1953), "Unchained Melody" (1955), and "The Poor People of Paris" (1956),  and is remembered for a version of "Sinner Man" (1956), definitively setting the sound with varying tempos, orchestral flourishes, and wailing background vocals.  "Unchained Melody" was the first million seller for Baxter and was awarded a gold disc.  "The Poor People of Paris" also sold over one million copies.  He also achieved success with concept albums of his own orchestral suites: Le Sacre Du Sauvage, Festival Of The Gnomes, Ports Of Pleasure, and Brazil Now, the first three for Capitol and the fourth on Gene Norman's Crescendo label.       ...    --  Wikipedia

posts.title: Blue Lights
posts.description:
https://youtu.be/9IK3hWlkJ08 


Kenny Burrell 

   "Blue Lights, Vol. 2" 


  ····   
ROCK SALT, CHUCKIN':
Louis Smith, Junior Cook, Tina Brooks, Kenny Burrell, Bobby Timmons, Sam Jones, Art Blakey.
THE MAN I LOVE:
Louis Smith, Kenny Burrell, Duke Jordan, Sam Jones, Art Blakey.
PHINUPI:
Louis Smith, Junior Cook, Kenny Burrell, Duke Jordan, Sam Jones, Art Blakey.
  ····   
THE "blowing session" (or "jam session" as it used to be called) is currently quite a ubiquitous commodity in the contemporary jazz recording industry. Musicians have always gathered to "jam" or "blow" with a minimum of preparation and preconceived  
ideas. And it was certainly a good idea, with the advent of recording equipment (and particularly the LP), to assembleand capture such sessions  —  this spontaneity of expression  —  on records. I think one must acknowledge that in the "blowing session" lies much of the unique and romantic flavor of jazz. It
has been argued, however, that the recorded "blowing session" has lately become, in many instances, even more formless, disorganized and undisciplined than its definition would imply.
And it has been said that the primary reasons for this are in the bringing together of musicians who are not in themselves disciplined  instrumentalists and/or who have not had sufficient playing experience with one another to have developed the sympathies and rapport required for their successful integration. A related point which has frequently been voiced and
which has, perhaps, even greater significance is that the recorded  "blowing session" has come to be regarded by many musicians as just "another gig"; that it demands only that one be there, have his say on a tired set of chords, and leave. Since jazz has advanced to the point where many believe it to warrant consideration as a serious and important medium of expression and creativity, the "blowing session", when these comments are applicable to it, may represent something of a regression.
But all of this does not always have to be the case and if the "blowing session" is assembled with thought, purpose and care  —  which I think these two volumes of "Blue Lights" were  —  its many inherent and otherwise only implicit values can be brought
to the fore and can offer a strong definition of much of what jazz is.
I think the opening track on Volume one, Burrell's Yes Baby, is a fine illustration of the exceptional jazz this context can produce. It is a growling, funky (in the best sense of that over-worked term) blues, and the key to its success is also what is at the center of any successful "blowing session" —  unanimity and a collective energy of expression and direction. After the mood setting "head" a succession of solos begin which contain a strong unity of purpose and in which one finds a related-to-the-group as well as an individual cohesiveness.
The majority of the musicians presented here have recorded previously for Blue Note. Twenty-seven year old guitarist and leader, Kenny Burrell, has proven that his flexible style (his experiences include gigs with Benny Goodman and Buck Clayton on up to Tony Scott, Jimmy Smith, etc.) fits comfortably and effectively within any jazz idiom or context. Several facets of his approach are in evidence here; his relaxed forcefulness on the blues (particularly on Yes Baby and Rock Salt) and his lyrical working over of a pretty popular song, Autumn In NewYork. On the latter tune, which offers a very good showcase for his talents, he builds an engaging melodic statement-embellishing  on the first chorus in a Johnny Smith-like chordal style and then improvising thoughtful lines on the chords. He is currently leading his own group at the Brankers Melody Room in New York City.
Trumpeter Louis Smith, also twenty-seven, may force, at this time, a comparison with Clifford Brown. But though his approach is strikingly similar to that of Brown's, he does have his own things to say and the equipment to say them well. His statements on Rock Salt and Man I Love (which seem to me to be among his best on record) show, apart from the open-emotion heatedness one has come to expect from him, a good sense of continuity and an adjectival restraint that is, perhaps, an indication of his growing control of this style which could make him a significant figure on his instrument. He is, at this writing, with Horace Silver.
Both Duke Jordan (thirty-six) and Bobby Timmons (twenty-three) belong to the line of pianists that has its roots in Art Tatum and Teddy Wilson. I think Jordan's most gratifying virtue lies in his ability to weave spare, uncluttered lines which can be very beautiful in their directness and simplicity. His qualities of sensitivity and lyricism have frequently been praised by musicians and some critics, but, perhaps because he is not a particularly imposing piano player, he has never acquired the large audience his talents deserve. And yet, listening to him here (especially on Scotch Blues-where he briefly employs an effective chordal style- and Phinupi) one hears that it is exactly his economically-calm conviction which is quickly.
and quietly (almost secretly), getting to the heart of the matter and getting some significant things said. Timmons' style contains elements of both Bud Powell and Horace Silver, but it would be unfair to pass him off as simply an imitator. He seems rather to have employed what he has learned from these men as a means of informing and enlarging his own conception and he delivers potent solos on Rock Salt, Caravan and Chuckin',
I think having Art Blakey on a session guarantees that it will swing. Blakey can inflame the most apathetic of groups (which this one isn't) and propell it far beyond its normal capacities.
His sympathies with the soloists are often uncanny and he himself  solos with more consistent meaning, and with fewer extraneous displays of vocabulary, than do certain of his similarly dexterous contemporaries. Thirty-nine years old, Blakey has, in recent years, been leading groups of "Jazz Messengers".
Bassist Sam Jones and tenors Junior Cook and Tina Brooks mark their initial Blue Note appearances with these albums. Jones, born in Jacksonville, Florida on November 12, 1924, worked with several rhythm and blues groups and led his own combo at the Harlem Club in Miami for three years, before moving to New York in 1949. He has an exceptionally strong rhythmic sense and is also capable of doing imaginative things with a melody. His work on Man I Love spotlights these talents well.
Cook and Brooks are two saxophonists of whom I think you will be hearing a great deal more in the future. Both are unusually forceful and fluent soloists whose conceptual foundations   are related, but who are otherwise quite different from each other. Cook posseses a round, full, rolling tone and approaches his lines in a manner that suggests the influences of
Wardell Gray and Sonny Rollins. An assured and inventive structuring can be heard in most of his solos here, particularly on Yes Baby and Rock Salt. Though there are occasional traces of Sonny Stitt in Cook's playing, a resemblance to Stitt is more immediately discernible in Brooks whose extensive experience with rhythm and blues bands has developed in him a strength and vitality of expression that are among his most significant attributes and which his statements on Chuckin' and Yes Baby illustrate. Cook was born in Pensacola, Florida on July 22, 1934; Brooks in North Carolina on June 7, 1932.
I think you will agree that the quality of these sets is above that of the average "blowing session". Just as important, I think, as the unusual consistency of good solos these volumes contain, is the work of the group as a whole. This is a session that went well and the musicians concerned seemed to have known that.  
  -- ROBERT LEVIN
For purposes of immediate identification, and particularly because the two tenors may not yet be familiar to the listener, there follows a solo-order chart below.
  ····   
VOLUME TWO (BLP 1597)
ROCK SALT; Smith, Cook, Burrell, Brooks, Timmons, Jones.
MAN I LOVE; Jones, Smith, Jordan, Jones.
CHUCKIN', Timmons, Burrell, Brooks, Smith, Cook, Jones (fours:
Burrell and three horns in same order as solos, with Blakey).
PHINUPI, Cook, Smith, Burrell, Jordan, Blakey.
  ····   
 (album notes) 


--------
Kenneth Earl Burrell (born July 31, 1931)  is an American jazz guitarist, singer and composer known for his work on numerous top jazz labels: Prestige, Blue Note, Verve, CTI, Muse, and Concord. His collaborations with Jimmy Smith were notable, and produced the 1965 Billboard Top Twenty hit Verve album Organ Grinder Swing.  Burrell has cited jazz guitarists Charlie Christian, Oscar Moore, and Django Reinhardt as influences, along with blues guitarists T-Bone Walker and Muddy Waters.

Laurindo Almeida Featuring Bud Shank

  "Brazilliance"  

····


I can still remember, and vividly too, the impression this music made upon me when it was first released by Pacific Jazz Records more than 30 years ago. West Coast jazz was in the first flower of its creativity; Dave Brubeck, Paul Desmond, Shorty Rogers, Art Pepper, Gerry Mulligan, Chet Baker and others were breaking new ground, or at least reinterpreting the jazz past in interesting, original ways, and each month, it seemed, we jazz fans were treated to one or more new musical delights from this nascent center of jazz creativity. Bud Shank was just beginning to emerge as one of the more dependably creative young performers on the Los Angeles scene, with a lilting, immediately recognizable alto sound that like several of his models had little to do with the almost inescapable influence of Charlie Parker, the then reigning jazz saxophonist. Still, the few recordings Shank had made several with Shorty Rogers, and the Pacific Jazz sessions with trombonists Bob Enevoldsen, Stu Williamson and Maynard Ferguson-despite the assurance
and decidedly lyrical bent of his playing, marking him as a player to watch, left many of us, I think, totally unprepared for the striking power and sheer loveliness of the music he created in tandem with Laurindo Almeida, the first fruits of which are offered in this marvelous, deeply satisfying album.
Make no mistake, The Laurindo Almeida Quartet (as the album was first titled) was something of an experimental album for its time, representing as it did the first successful fusion of American jazz and traditional Brazilian music. Most of us jazz fans of the time had heard nothing like it before; few Americans in fact had even heard any authentic Brazilian folk-based music of the sort that Almeida brought to the sessions. So, it was ear-opening, not only in terms of the song materials and the easy, infectious rhythms underlying them, but also in light of the soaring, incandescent clarity of Shank's playing, revealing for the first time the full extent of his fast-maturing conception, which meshed flawlessly with Almeida's commanding, effortless-sounding acoustic guitar and the beguiling arrangements he had fashioned for the group.
On its release the album caused something of a quiet sensation in jazz circles. It was widely praised in the jazz press for the freshness and audacity of its conception, the all-but-perfect way the two musics had been brought into beautiful, fruitful alignment no less than the flawless playing of the principals. Along with the Gerry Mulligan Quartet,
the Chet Baker Quartet and the John Lewis-Bill Perkins Grand Encounter sessions, the Almeida-Shank collaborations on this album take their place among the classic Pacific Jazz recordings.
Now, it should not be forgotten that in previous years jazz had incorporated Latin rhythms in various ways, Dizzy Gillespie's and George Shearing's efforts in these directions being good examples of the successful use of Afro-Cuban rhythmic elements in a jazz context, and others could be cited as well. However, what distinguished the present performances from these and like efforts was the fact that the Almeida quartet had taken a subtly different tack, in essence approaching matters from the other side, laying in jazz over what was essentially a program of authentic Brazilian music, retaining the character of the latter while adding to it the colors, inflections and improvisational flavor of jazz. "The idea of putting samba and jazz together was different," Almeida recalled, adding, "As long as samba is in 2%, and jazz is a la breve, why not put the two together?" In consequence, the results were more than subtly different from those earlier attempts at this sort of fusion. Shank's graceful contributions notwithstanding, Almeida was the real linchpin of this musical experiment. After all, it was he who brought the bulk of the repertoire to it, crafted the arrangements used by the group and who, as a Brazilian musician with wide familiarity with his country's native music, was the ultimate arbiter of the musical authenticity of the group's approach. A native of Sao Paulo, where he was born in 1917, Almeida at the time of these recordings was highly regarded as a classical guitar virtuoso who had made a number of recordings of this music (as he continued to do in subsequent years). Paralleling his classical activities the guitarist had had extensive experience in Brazilian popular music as well, performing on radio and in nightclubs in Rio de Janeiro. American listeners first became aware of his formidable talents in 1947 when he came to the U.S. to join the Stan Kenton Orchestra as a featured soloist, following which he involved himself in studio recording activities and led various groups in the Los Angeles area where he settled.
The present group was an outgrowth of a trio the guitarist had been leading in late 1952 at the 881 Club in Hollywood. Replacing the group's regular bassist, the veteran Harry Babasin began performing duets with Almeida on Brazilian choros, adding to their baiao, butuque and samba rhythms the syncopations of jazz. This evolved gradually, the bassist recalled, for "during the evening Laurindo would play several sets of solo guitar, and rather than just hang around the bar or take a walk, I found myself joining him on bass." At Babasin's urging, Almeida soon joined him in a series of rehearsal sessions with Shank, and drummer Roy Harte in the back room of the latter's Drum City, an instrument store in Hollywood. "We rehearsed for about a month," Harte recalled. "It was Harry's idea, and his bass parts provided the lead rhythmically."
"Actually, we rehearsed for our own education," he continued, "to see whether Laurindo would swing. Of course, we all knew how great he was as a formal guitarist, but we wanted to find out if he could really swing in jazz. The whole thing was to combine the baiao beat with jazz. That was what we were aiming at a jazz baiao [because] the samba was considered corny then. Our main purpose was to achieve the light, swinging feel of the baiao-combined with jazz blowing. In order to get this, I played brushes on a conga drum, not a snare drum. This gave it a light feeling. Actually, I was trying to play with my right hand to Bud's jazz blowing, and with my left I was putting in the samba color with Laurindo's
playing."
Once the four musicians had worked out a satisfactory approach to, in Babasin's words, "a combination of samba rhythm and jazz, played with a free, light, loose feeling," and developed a repertoire of sufficient breadth, they approached Richard Bock, then serving as talent booker for The Haig, one of Los Angeles' leading jazz clubs of the period, and were engaged to perform there one night a week, during which they tightened up their collective performing skills, refined their arrangements and playing formats and expanded their repertoire further. Bock, who had established Pacific Jazz Records less than a year earlier and was
experiencing great success with the first recordings of the Gerry Mulligan Quartet, which also had come into being at The Haig, quickly agreed to record the group. In April of 1953, at two separate sessions held a week apart, the Laurindo Almeida Quartet undertook its first recordings. The results were initially released on two 10" Pacific Jazz albums, LP 7 and LP 13, and were later combined onto a single 12" disc, LP 1204. The alternate version of Speak Low, included here, was first released on the compilation album Jazz West Coast, Vol. 1 (JWC 500).
As you'll hear, the results were uniformly felicitous, and the experiment must be counted an unqualified success. Not only had Almeida selected the repertoire wisely (only the standards Stairway To The Stars and Speak Low, jazz composer Dick Hazzard's Hazardous and Babasin's Noctambulism deviate from the all-Brazilian cast of the remainder of the song program) but had devised a series of arrangements that while remaining faithful to the authentic character of the folk-based song materials, skillfully integrated the jazz elements that Shank, Babasin and Harte brought to the music, framing their talents perfectly in short, at least in the context of this music, where real individuality of expression was subsumed by the larger goals. Despite the beauty and originality of the music it created, a prior commitment prevented the group's Haig engagement being extended. Unable to find a replacement of anywhere near his abilities, the three Americans reluctantly disbanded and went their separate ways. Here ends its first chapter, with the next, five years in the future, to be taken up in the second volume of the Brazilliance recordings.
-- Pete Welding

Mantovani 

       "The Magic Of Mantovani; Mantovani's Golden Hits" 


  ····   

RECORD ONE
The Magic of MANTOVANI
  ····   
MANTOVANI'S
GOLDEN HITS
  ····   
Annunzio Paolo Mantovani, a violinist who is the
son of a violinist, always wanted to lead an orchestra
with a lot of strings. And when a recording company.
offered him just such an orchestra in 1951, he determined  to give his strings such a distinctive sound that they would be immediately recognizable. How well he succeeded in doing that can be seen in the fact that, after almost a quarter of a century and  innumerable attempts by others to capture the elusive Mantovani quality, there is still only one "Mantovani sound." More than a million copies of his albums are bought every year. And his annual, three-month  American tours covering 60 cities, which he began in 1956, have sold an unprecedented number of tickets for a concert attraction.
Born in Italy, but brought to England when he was four, Mantovani ("Monty," to his English friends) began  playing professionally when he was sixteen and two years later began leading his own groups which have ranged from quartets and restaurant orchestras to the 45-piece concert ensemble (including 32 strings) with which he records and tours.
The secret of his continued success, he says, is that he is "a string man." "I know what I want from string players," he explains. "I know the capabilities of the violin. I know what it can do.
"And," he adds with a knowing smile. "I've got first class lads playing for me.
  ····   
SIDE ONE
  ····   
Charmaine
Rapée-Pollack
This was the record that changed Mantovani from a
successful English conductor into an international phenomenon. In 1951, when the American branch of Mantovani's English recording firm asked him to record an album of waltzes, he decided use a big string section.
"I wanted to get a classic string sound, to use close
of sound, harmonies, to get an effect of an overlapping as though we were in a cathedral," he later explained.
The Mantovani string sound was born in this album.
One of the album's waltzes, "Charmaine," caught the ear of a Cleveland disc jockey, Bill Randle, who plugged the song, making it — and Mantovani — a tremendous hit.
  ····   
Greensleeves
Traditional-Arranged by Binge
This old familiar ballad dates back at least to the 16th century. Mantovani's fondness for it is reflected in the fact that he named his country home in Bournemouth "Greensleeves." This arrangement, originally recorded in 1953 but since re-recorded, is by Ronald Binge, a composer and arranger who worked with Mantovani in creating the inimitable Mantovani sound
  ····   
Diane
Rapée
A logical follow-up to the ground-breaking success of Mantovani's "Charmaine" was "Diane." "Charmaine," written by Erno Rapée and Lew Pollack, had been the springboard for Mantovani's fame and had launched the fad for motion-picture theme songs in the late  Twenties. The song was not heard in the film itself (What Price Glory, a silent picture), but used to advertise it.
The following year, Rapée wrote "Diane," which was
part of the soundtrack of Seventh Heaven, starring
Charles Farrell and Janet Gaynor, who won the 
Academy Award for her performance.
  ····   
Swedish Rhapsody
Alfven
This bright, merry tune, which Mantovani fills with
orchestra bells, a gay accordion and bubbling flute and clarinet, is taken from music by Hugo Alfven which was based on Swedish folk material. Mantovani's version shows how easily he can switch from his familiar string sounds to an almost boisterous use of woodwinds and brass without really getting out of character.
  ····   
Around the World
Young
Still another variation of Mantovani's use of strings is
developed in this arrangement of Victor Young's theme for the 1956 film Around the World in 80 Days. Opening with a high, singing trumpet solo, Mantovani features the trumpet all the way through, cushioning it on his strings in the second chorus.
  ····   
Main Theme from "Exodus"
Gold
Ernest Gold's score for Otto Preminger's film Exodus
was one of the commanding musical achievements for films in 1960. To write the score, Gold, a Hollywood composer, spent months in Israel getting the feeling of the country, the people and their music. This prize-winning theme was adapted from several traditional Hebrew tunes, blended and developed by Gold to catch the underlying feeling of Israel. Mantovani underscores that feeling by the way in which he builds from a gentle, almost wistful beginning to the staunch, forceful statement of the end.
  ····   
SIDE TWO
Something To Remember You By
Dietz-Schwartz
There are — or can be — three aspects of "Something To
Remember You By." It can be romantic, as Mantovani
plays it. It can be torchy, as Libby Holman sang it in
Three's a Crowd, a 1930 revue. Or it can be comedy,
which is the way Howard Dietz and Arthur Schwartz
intended i to be when they wrote it and the
way Rudy Vallee wound up singing it in 1931. The original "crooner" was trying to sing it in a romantic-torchy way in a Boston theater when a grapefruit came sailing
out of the balcony at him, landing on the drummer's
cymbal. The incident made front pages across the country, and Vallee kept the publicity going for months by singing the song with a wastebasket over his head.
  ····   
Love Makes the World Go 'Round (La Ronde)
Straus-Cochran-Ducreaux
The heritage and almost the name of the great waltz-composing Strausses of Vienna was carried on by Oscar Straus, born in Vienna in 1870. He is known best for his operetta The Chocolate Soldier and, in the waltzing tradition, "A Waltz Dream." "Love Makes the World Go 'Round" is a Straus waltz composed for a French film, La Ronde, known originally as Merry-Go-Round, a title Mantovani acknowledges with the merry-go-round music style that turns up in the middle of this arrangement. The melody became known as "Love Makes the World Go 'Round " when English lyrics were written
for it by Dorcas Cochran.
  ····   
Unchained Melody
North
Of all the younger American composers who were writing 
 "serious" music just after World War II, Alex North
was one of the most promising. In a field in which 
newcomers are rarely well-known, his name was already
familiar and, partly because of that, he was called to
Hollywood to write the score for the film version of
A Streetcar Named Desire. It was a score that made
striking use of jazz, blues and other idiomatic American
music, a score set so brilliantly apart from most film
scores of the day that North was kept on to write scores
for another Tennessee Williams film, The Rose Tatoo,
Arthur Miller's Death of a Salesman, Carson McCuller's
Member of the Wedding, as well as such sheer Hollywoodiana as Cleopatra, The Agony and the Ecstasy and
Viva Zapata! These scores served their purposes well
but none of them produced a melody that caught the public fancy until he composed a title tune for a film called Unchained in 1955.
  ····   
Fascination
Marchetti
This is a valse tzigane — a gypsy waltz — and Mantovani puts it immediately into character with a solo violin coaxing out the melody in gypsy style. It was composed relatively recently in 1904 by F. D. Marchetti but remained a esoteric part of the light classical repertoire until 1957 when it was used as a recurring theme in a film called Love in the Afternoon which starred Gary Cooper, Audrey Hepburn and Maurice Chevalier. It became a hit then, not because of the film, but because of a record by Jane Morgan, an American who had made a name as a singer in Paris and found in this old romantic waltz a song with which she could transfer her continental flair to her native country.
  ····   
This Nearly Was Mine
Rodgers-Hammerstein
Richard Rodgers wrote only two songs for the mature French planter, Emile de Becque, in South Pacific — "Some Enchanted Evening" and "This Nearly Was
Mine." But with only these two songs, Ezio Pinza, the
great operatic basso making his first appearance in the Broadway musical theater, became the matinee idol of 1949. Rodgers wrote both songs as explanations of
de Becque's character-"romantic, rather powerful, but
not too involved," as he explained. And this was the
way that Pinza sang them. But Mantovani sees "This
Nearly Was Mine" as a gentle, almost wistful song and the attitude is set in the very opening passages by the woodwinds.
  ····   
The Blue Danube
Strauss-Arranged by Mantovani
After Mantovani had his first great success in 1951 with "Charmaine," a single taken from an album of waltzes, it was inevitable that there should be, as a follow-up, another album of waltzes. So, in 1952, he put together a second-this time a collection by one of his favorite composers, Johann Strauss, the younger. Naturally, the album included the most famous of all the Strauss waltzes, possibly the most famous waltz ever written: "The Blue Danube."    ... 
   (album notes)

      Annunzio Paolo Mantovani (Italian: [anˈnuntsjo ˈpaːolo mantoˈvaːni]; 15 November 1905 – 30 March 1980) was an Italian British conductor, composer and light orchestra–styled entertainer with a cascading strings musical signature.

The book British Hit Singles & Albums stated that Mantovani was "Britain's most successful album act before the Beatles ... the first act to sell over one million stereo albums and [have] six albums simultaneously in the US Top 30 in 1959". 

Mantovani was born on 15 November 1905 in Venice, Italy, into a musical family.    ...    --  Wikipedia

Once the four musicians had worked out a satisfactory approach to, in Babasin's words, "a  combination of samba rhythm and jazz, played with a free, light, loose feeling," and developed a repertoire of sufficient breadth, they approached Richard Bock, then serving as talent booker for The Haig, one of Los Angeles' leading jazz clubs of the period, and were engaged to perform there one night a week, during which they tightened up their collective performing skills, refined their arrangements and playing formats and expanded their repertoire further. Bock, who had established Pacific Jazz Records less than a year earlier and was
experiencing great success with the first recordings of the Gerry Mulligan Quartet, which also had come into being at The Haig, quickly agreed to record the group. In April of 1953, at two separate sessions held a week apart, the Laurindo Almeida Quartet undertook its first recordings. The results were initially released on two 10" Pacific Jazz albums, LP 7 and LP 13, and were later combined onto a single 12" disc, LP 1204. The alternate version of Speak Low, included here, was first released on the compilation album Jazz West Coast, Vol. 1 (JWC 500).
As you'll hear, the results were uniformly felicitous, and the experiment must be counted an unqualified success. Not only had Almeida selected the repertoire wisely (only the standards Stairway To The Stars and Speak Low, jazz composer Dick Hazzard's Hazardous and Babasin's Noctambulism deviate from the all-Brazilian cast of the remainder of the song program) but had devised a series of arrangements that while remaining faithful to the authentic character of the folk-based song materials, skillfully integrated the jazz elements that Shank, Babasin and Harte brought to the music, framing their talents perfectly in short, at least in the context of this music, where real individuality of expression was subsumed by the larger goals. The resultant synthesis, and that's what it truly is, is thoroughly, winningly graceful in character, the sinuous rhythms and charmingly lyrical qualities of the Brazilian song materials, unfamiliar and unobtrusively "exotic" to American listeners of the time, always uppermost in Almeida's mind, preserved in, even dominating the guitarist's controlled, lucid, elegant settings, most of which had been fully worked out in virtually all of their component parts, the only exceptions being Shank's warm, lucent improvisations.
Despite the beauty and originality of the music it created, a prior commitment prevented the group's Haig engagement being extended. And while Shank, Harte and especially Babasin felt they had created a worthwhile jazz offshoot of real attractiveness and commercial potential, and wanted to persevere with it by seeking playing engagements outside the Los Angeles area, the guitarist demurred. Having gained a solid toehold in the city's film and commercial music recording studios and also desirous of continuing with his career as a concert guitarist, Almeida decided to remain in Los Angeles. Unable to find a replacement of anywhere near his abilities, the three Americans reluctantly disbanded and went their separate ways. Here ends its first chapter, with the next, five years in the future, to be taken up in the second volume of the Brazilliance recordings.

Lew Davies And His Orchestra

"Delicado"



Be very careful when you listen to this record.
It is going to take all of your attention.
It is going to involve you in a positive act of listening.
It is going to make you an actual member of the team of creative musicians and creative engineers who took part in the initial stages of this recording. You — the creative listener — will complete the process.
Not since the release of the first volume of the precedent-shattering Persuasive Percussion series has a recording revealed such fascinating new potentials in phonographic reproduction as this significant Lew Davies creation, Delicado. 
  ····   
DELICADO
SOFT, SUBTLE, SOPHISTICATED, SOUNDS
LEW DAVIES AND HIS ORCHESTRA
  ····   
When Command Records issued the first PERSUASIVE PERCUSSION album, it revealed an amazing new relationship between brilliant musicianship and adventurous, exploratory engineering techniques. This was an association that had occasionally tried to meet on an equal footing in past decades when the art of sound reproduction was still in an elementary stage. But following the astounding break-throughs in sound engineering that occurred in the late Nineteen Fifties (many of which were accomplished by Command's engineers), Enoch Light of Command Records was the first producer of records to realize that this new era of sound reproduction could also mean a new era of music-music that was created with the deliberate intention of taking advantage
of the vast new range of colors and timbres that the astonishing advances in engineering techniques now made possible.
The first result of this pioneering meeting of inventive musical skill and painstaking engineering craftsmanship was PERSUASIVE PERCUSSION  —  a recording so completely original and so overwhelmingly valid in conception
that it had an incredibly shattering effect on the entire recording industry, changing concepts and procedures that had been taken for granted for many years and opening what amounted to a totally new field of recording activity.
The succeeding volumes of PERSUASIVE
PERCUSSION that followed that first one, as well as the PROVOCATIVE PERCUSSION series that Enoch Light also produced and conducted, were often startling in the effects that were obtained. 
The bright, penetrating brilliance of the  
high notes and the awesome depth and solidity of the lows were commented on with delighted amazement by critics and
non-professional listeners alike. The shocking impact of massed ensembles, the startling juxtaposition of highs and lows that would normally have been impossible to reproduce with full-bodied clarity, made these recordings an extraordinarily stimulating adventure   — an adventure that picked the listener up and carried him along on a kaleidoscopic wave of constantly changing excitement.
But despite the excitement that is generated by these recordings, listening to them is essentially a passive act. Because the presentation is so overwhelming, because it is presented in such a strongly overt manner, the listener has scarcely any alternative except to hold onto his seat and let wave upon wave of musical exhilaration strike him. His contribution
to the cycle of performance, reproduction and reception is simply to be there when the music is being reproduced.
Now, with DELICADO, we come to something else 
 — something else entirely — something that is as revolutionary in its own way as
PERSUASIVE PERCUSSION was in its way.
Once again the basic concept is the exploitation of the full potentials of brilliant musicianship and the most advanced discoveries of Command's sound engineers (which, needless to say, have continued to advance since theinitial appearance of PERSUASIVE PERCUSSION). In DELICADO, however, the objective has not been to startle or to shock. Amazement was one of the reactions produced by those earlier recordings and it is a reaction that is also 
generated by DELICADO. But this time it is a different kind of amazement because the approach in DELICADO is almost exactly the opposite of that in the two PERCUSSION series.
In DELICADO, as the title implies, the tone and style is one of delicacy, of subtlety, of absorbing fusions of rich, warm sounds, tantalizing timbres and evocatively haunting melodies.
The succeeding volumes of PERSUASIVE
PERCUSSION that followed that first one,  
 as well as the PROVOCATIVE PERCUSSION series that Enoch Light also produced and conducted, were often startling in the effects that were obtained. The bright, penetrating brilliance of the high notes and the awesome depth and solidity of the lows were commented on with delighted amazement by critics and non-professional listeners alike. The shocking impact of massed ensembles, the startling juxtaposition of highs and lows that would normally have been impossible to reproduce
Originated and Produced by Enoch Light.
This is music that, in its smooth, sinuous softness, actually demands more of the musicians, 
the sound engineer, the playback equipment 
and the listener than the more forthright and  relatively obvious style of the PERCUSSION series.  These are subtle sounds you hear  —  notes that are beautifully turned and polished to a lustre that can only be fully appreciated by the listener who contributes something positive of himself to the listening process. These are sounds to be savored as one would savor a vintage wine — sounds to be reflected on as one would reflect on the subtle interrelationships in a great painting — 
sounds to be lived with as one enriches one's 
 existence with a masterpiece of furniture design.
And yet while it may be true that these are sounds for a connoisseur, for a sophisticated listener, these are also sounds that can make a sophisticated listener. This is music that, subtle as it may be, still communicates to anyone who cares to listen — to actively listen. In this process of listening lies the germ of a true appreciation of the beauties that are waiting to be discovered in such a sensitive  
 blending of music, precision engineering and the
involvement of the human spirit that make up
DELICADO.
  ····   
SIDE ONE
ALONE TOGETHER. Gently and seductively,
this Arthur Schwartz and Howard Dietz classic
is introduced by an inviting bass clarinet
figure, on the left, that is picked up by Doc
Severinsen's muted trumpet, on the right. The
subtle conjunction of timbres of the flute, 
 carrying the melody, and the bass clarinet 
 continuing its figure establishes the exotic mood
of Lew Davies' arrangement. Notice the sense
of openness and increasing involvement that
is created when the two flutes follow the softly
muted trumpet and produce an expansion of
sound that is totally different from that of the
single flute that preceded the trumpet.
PRELUDE TO A KISS. The suavely sophisticated
feeling of this arrangement hangs on
the sensitive use of Bob Haggart's walking
bass which establishes a neatly shaded 
 foundation on which the softly 
 sibilant qualities of the woodwinds 
 and the brass can be
exchanged. The gorgeous blending of the four
muted trombones, played by Urbie Green,
Bobby Byrne, Jack Satterfield and Paul Faulice,
add an incredible richness to the smooth
texture of this treatment.
C'EST SI BON. As a change of pace, Lew
Davies brings a lively and witty tone to his sly
evolvement of this Parisian favorite. He
declares his intentions in his bright, humorous
use of bongo and bassoon on the left in the
introductory passages. And he carries them out
in his entertaining balancing of piccolo aver
bassoon and bongo and the subsequent
doubling up of the piccolos, a tactic which 
— like the doubling of flutes
  on ALONE TOGETHER —  
brings an incredibly subtle change in the
space relationship of the music. Notice how he
also interweaves descending figures for the
bassoon and clarinets and the sudden, startling
contrast in the appearance of a strong
stentorian trombone passage. The piece is
cappd by a brilliantly low and exquisitely
meaty trombone blurt.
SOFT LIGHTS AND SWEET MUSIC. Delicate
shading spreads through this arrangement like
ripples on a pond. It starts with Tony Mottola
pensively stroking his guitar while the woodwinds
trace out a descending figure. Then the
trombones pick up the melody with an imposing
sound that stretches and stretches until
it covers the full listening spectrum while the
vibes add a shimmering quality of their own.
Don't overlook the deftly woven mixture of the
strikingly complementary timbres of the alto
flute and a bucket-muted trumpet that occurs
in the second chorus.
THE WAY YOU LOOK TONIGHT. Lew Davies
lends a hand (or, more accurately, a finger) in
establishing the introductory figure, played
first by guitar and single-noted piano (Davies)
in unison and then developed by the clarinets.
This idea is carried on into the melody, first
within the melodic line and then as a supporting
fill for Doc Severinsen's muted trumpet.
and Tony Mottola's guitar. The remarkably
close-up, rough-grained alto saxophone  
solo is played by Walt Levinsky.
THE BOY NEXT DOOR. The willowy magic of
Stanley Webb's alto flute brings this lovely
tune into being, setting a reflective, moody
quality that is picked up by the trombones and
the other woodwinds. When the clarinets take
over in the second chorus, there is a superb
example of the delicacy that a brass instrument
can contribute to a background in the
sensitive way in which Doc Severinsen's muted
trumpet noodles along under the clarinets.
  ····   
SIDE TWO
AND THE ANGELS SING. These angels swag
ger while they sing. The swagger is injected
by the finger-snapping that Lew Davies adds
to Bobby Rosengarden's vibes in the opening
and by the cutting, growling blast with which
Doc Severinsen's trumpet answers the sonorous
trombones. The contrast of rich mellowness
(exemplified in Urbie Green's trombone
solo) and pin-pricking rhythmic pulsation
underlies the entire development of the piece
right through the final fading melange.
WHAT'S NEW. Soft, supple subtlety flows
through this gorgeous creation. Its character
is established in the deep, introductory woodwinds,
made positive by Stanley Webb's gently
singing flute and filled out by the lustrous
sound of the trombone ensemble. The range of
nuances that are used throughout this 
  arrangement is all the more amazing 
 because it is accomplished in the calmest 
 and most unruffled of manners.
ONE FOR MY BABY. This Harold Arlen favorite
digs in with a sensuously provocative beat
established by Tony Mottola's guitar and Don
Lamond's brushes. A lost, after-hours mood
hangs over the piece as the dark-tinged wood
winds, the deep-hued trombones and Doc
Severinsen's edgily muted trumpet mull
through the melody. Except for the trumpet,
there is a concentration on dark, shadowy
sounds that is particularly notable in the way
Joe Palmer's bassoon underlines the muted
trumpet.
THE SOFT SELL The underplayed and the
implied, which are of the essence in DELICADO,
have served as the inspiration for this
composition by Enoch Light and Lew Davies
which exemplifies the suave use of subtle.
sounds. It's worth noting that softness and
subtlety do not preclude the appearance of
sharp, impinging sounds. Actually, the skillful
use of such sounds is almost essential — notice
the way Tony Mottola's guitar cuts in under the
trombones, how the bongos add a clarity to
the lines of the introduction and how even the
woodwinds contribute bright, lightening jabs
under the trombones in the second chorus.
NOW IS THE HOUR. Stanley Webb turns to
the distinctive timbre of the recorder, backed
by Tony Mottola's ukulele-tuned guitar, to
weave the atmospheric texture of this Maori
song. A very unusual and striking combination
of instruments occurs at the beginning of the
second chorus when Bobby Rosengarden's
vibes are accompanied by Stanley Webb's bass
clarinet, a mixture of high and low transients
that blend into a fascinatingly exotic effect.
TAKE IT EASY. Going out brightly, Lew Davies
concludes this essay in delicacy with an 
example of peppery gentility that is prodded.
along first by Doc Severinsen's exquisite
muted trumpet and later by Phil Bodner's
piping piccolo (which shortly picks up Joe
Palmer's bassoon as a sonic balance). The
clean precision with which both Bodner and
Palmer play and Command's engineers catch
the full value of every sound is brilliantly demonstrated in the very last two notes 
 — one from the piccolo, the other
 from the bassoon — 
  each played and recorded 
 with neatly clipped clarity.
(album notes)

Lew Davies
Born 25 September 1911, Ashland, Kentucky.
Died 11 December 1968, New York City, New York.
There's almost no trace left of Lew Davies except for his arrangements on the "Persuasive Percussion" series and most of the rest of Command's records. Enoch Light certainly contributed the inspiration and technical genius behind the Command style, but Davies, not Light, receives the arranger credit on the majority of Command's releases.

Davies attended the Cincinnati Conservatory of Music and later studied composition with the noted teacher, Tibor Serly. He began arranging for dance bands in 1928 and worked in radio as well. He was hired by Enoch Light in the late 1950s and soon became Light's primary arranger. Many of the early Command releases include one or two original compositions by Davies, and the label released five albums under his own name. He also snuck in one album for Columbia, but is only credited in passing in the liner notes.

Although he primarily collaborated with Light, Davies did occasional arrangements for Lawrence Welk, Perry Como, and Lena Horne. Davies' arrangements hit a nice balance between showing off stereo effects and creating a genuine musical mood, and are among the more listenable recordings from the stereo showcase period.   ...

During the 1950s, the group continued to make live appearances with the same personnel, but their RCA Victor recording sessions would often have studio musicians substituting for one or another, because keyboardist Artie Dunn did not read music and guitarist Al Nevins became much more interested in the production end of the record business. Phineas Newborn Jr.

  "Here Is Phineas (The Piano Artistry Of Phineas Newborn Jr.)"


····

HERE IS PHINEAS
THE PIANO ARTISTRY OF PHINEAS NEWBORN JR.
····
For years now I've listened to people scream at me about unknown pianists they have discovered. "He's greater than Bud". "He cuts Oscar". "He leaves Tatum standing still". As many times as I have heard these cries, that is how often I have been disappointed. Invariably, these unknowns are, at their best, simply minor talents, and, at their worst, pale copies of great pianists.
About a year ago I began to hear stories about a fantastic pianist in Memphis, Tenn. with the almost quaint sounding name of Phineas Newborn, Jr. Men I respected, such as John Hammond, Willard Alexander and, of course, Count Basie, among many others, insisted that I must hear this guy. Due to my previous sad experiences, I could not get excited. However, when I got a chance to really hear Phineas in Storyville, for the first time I was not disappointed. The unknown had lived up to his press notices.
Phineas Newborn, Jr. was born December 14, 1932 in Memphis, Tenn. I believe this makes him all of 23 years old at the recording of this album. In all my years of listening to music I have never encountered a musician of such tender years who had such a fantastic command of his instrument. Perhaps my reaction to Phineas can be traced to my personal concern with the piano.
If this was my only reason for liking him, then I say it would be sufficient, for to my knowledge the only pianist who has as great, or greater command of the
piano is Art Tatum.
Phineas is a two-handed pianist, as opposed to the tendency of modern pianists to dwell on the single finger, right-hand style. The only time he can be accused of being a one-handed pianist is when he puts his right hand in his pocket and plays two choruses of a ballad, such as Embraceable You, exclusively with his left hand. Unfortunately, he does not do this in this album, but when you see him in person, ask him to play a left-handed solo for you. His left hand is developed to such an extent that he can and does execute any passage or chord with his left hand that he would do with his right. When you realize that he has the fastest right hand of anyone since Tatum (he might even exceed Tatum for sheer speed), then you get an idea of just what happens.
However, technique is only one facet of music. What of Phineas basic musical style? From whence does he come and where is he going?
First, let me warn the reader of what not to do upon first hearing Phineas. Do not be so overpowered by his technique that you neglect to listen to the music he plays. Through all his technical intricacies I hear a wonderful musical mind, a mind that without copying has absorbed the music of the jazz masters. I get a funny feeling when I hear Phineas. I concentrate on his fantastically "Bird"-influenced ideas and then I can't help but get the feeling that at any moment he is going to swing right into a Waller-James P. Johnson stride piano effect. He never quite does and I sometimes wish he would.
Phineas says his first jazz idols were Bird, Dizzy and Bud Powell. Later on, after he had begun to develop his own style, he heard Tatum. There is no doubt of the influence that these men left on Phineas. There is also evidence that he has listened to Erroll Garner.
However, there is never a question that Phineas has a unique approach to music. (In this album I believe Dahoud comes the closest to defining the Phineas Newborn style).
The only real criticism I have of his playing can be traced to his immaturity, both musically and in years.
He tends to want to play everything in the same tempo.
To be more explicit, he feels so relaxed at up-tempos that even in ballads he resorts to double-timing in order to utilize his technique. Also, he has a few figures of which he is fond. These appear a little too often in his playing. As soon as Phineas gets over the idea that he must create an impression the first time around the nightclub circuit, I am sure these minor faults will disappear.
Biographically, Phineas' history is not startling. The son of Phineas Newborn, Sr., a fine drummer and band leader in Memphis, he and his brother, Calvin, one year his junior, had an early musical beginning (Calvin plays guitar in the Phineas Newborn Quartet and is heard on some of the sides in this album). Phineas started the study of piano at the age of six with the pianist in his father's band. He continued right through high school, where he took up the study of brass instruments (trumpet, tuba, baritone horn, French horn). Later on, he learned the vibes, and in college and the Army he acquired the baritone, tenor and alto saxophones. Those who have heard him say he is nearly as fantastic on
these various instruments as he is on the piano. Fortunately, Phineas has concentrated on piano and does not try to impress us with his versatility.
His formal education, in addition to graduating from the Memphis School System, consists of two years as a music major at Tenn. A & I. Later on he spent a year at Lemoyne College in Memphis, before he was drafted into the Army in August 1953. He was discharged in June 1955, and played with his father's band until last month when he made the break after the Willard Alexander agency convinced him he should come North and let the world hear his talent. Jimmy Forrest 

     "Forrest Fire" 

  ····   
  
There was, and perhaps still is, a place on Howard
Street in Chicago where a lot of us used to go, called
the Bar of Music. The quartet-in-residence (although they never would have referred to themselves in that way, never having heard of the Lenox School) calledthemselves the Four Shades of Rhythm. The makeup of the group was piano, bass, electric guitar and conga drum, and the conga drummer was also a vocalist capable of at least an octave and a half below Billy Eckstine. The Bar o' Music was a nice place to go eitherwith a girl or a couple of friends, depending on your mood, and once you had been there often enough, it took on several of the better aspects of a private club.
You could meet your friends there  —  a few of them
were always sure to be around  —  the bartender knew what you wanted to drink without having to be reminded, the room itself was pleasant and dark, andthere was, of course, the music. The group had its specialties, two or three numbers which were requested time after time by those who represented the hard core of the clientele. One of them was a vocal version of Victor Young's A Hundred Years From Today, which has a lyric with just the right kind of pragmatic fatalism for two or three in the morning. And there was also, and always unannounced, a mysterious tenor saxophonist who would walk in suddenly, wearing a raccoon coat and cossack cap in whatever weather, blow a couple of startling choruses of whatever tune the Shades happened to be playing at the moment, and disappear again until the next time, which might be in an hour or two weeks.
The point to all of this is not that Jimmy Forrest or
his rhythm section ever appeared at the Bar o' Music —  more than likely they never have  —  but that small group, so-called "mainstream" jazz of the type they play here has its breeding-ground in clubs just like that one all over the country. To go even further, the novelist Ralph Ellison, in a brilliant essay on Charlie Christian that appeared in Saturday Review some time back, advanced the theory that the men we regard as the great innovators-Christian, Lester Young, Charlie Parker, etc.  —  may not truly be innovators in the most exact sense at all, but collators and organizers of various ideas played by local musicians of their areas  —  men who might really be the innovators, and of whom we will never hear. It was, of course, not Ellison's intent to detract from the stature of those men  —  and it would,
by now, be impossible even to attempt such a task  —  but simply to place the matter in perspective, and return   the music to the social situation from which it comes.
The quartet here is made up of tenor sax, organ,
guitar and drums, and represents a heightening of the elements that can be found in the local clubs. The use of organ is probably not only a matter of taste, but rather of acquired taste that has come from practical necessity. In the first place, the pianos in small clubs are, almost as a matter of tradition, invariably out of tune. And in the second place, if you have a good organist, you don't need a bass player, which makes one less person for the wandering tenorman to contend with when he comes to town. Which brings something  to mind. It might help in placing this album in its exact context to view it as a situation in which a visiting tenorman works with the local group. A fiction, of course, but possibly a helpful one.
The tenorman in question is Jimmy Forrest, and his
experience ranges over practically the entire jazz spectrum. The list of men he has worked with  —  Fate Marable, Jay McShann, Andy Kirk, and Duke Ellington are included  —  would make a good starting point for anyone's history of small, medium, and big-band jazz, and it is undoubtedly just that experience that made him such a valuable part of the Prestige Blues-Swingers on their album called Outskirts of Town (Prestige 7145).
But of course, you just don't step into company like the men listed above. Jimmy who was born in St. Louis on January 24, 1920, received his first formal musical education from Major N. Clark Smith, a member of the St. Louis educational system who had led various Army bands in World War I, and also happened to be an African prince. There was always music in the home  —  both Jimmy's parents were musicians-and his first regular gig came at the age of twelve, when he was a member of his mother's local band. From his beginnings   with Eva Forrest's Stompers, we go past the various other big bands, through a group he led with Curtis Fuller, Red Garland, George Joyner and Charlie Persip, to the current quintet he shares with Harry Edison.
None of this experience, though, would necessarily
prepare Jimmy to work with an organ (although he recorded with Jack McDuff on Prestige 7185), and when asked how he felt about it, he said, "It gives you more scope. You feel like you have a big band behind you."
He plays like a big-band tenor here, too in contrast tohis more restrained work with McDuff. There are
several possible reasons for Jimmy's change of approach, all interesting to speculate on. It might just have been the difference in the way a man feels from one day to the next. Or, it might have been his skill in adapting himself to the men he works with  —  a travelling musician would certainly have to do that, and his new way of playing blends as precisely with Larry Young as the gentler approach did with Jack McDuff.
Or, it just might have been the unconscious assertiveness that goes on in someone's mind when he becomes the leader of a record date for the first time.
Having mentioned Larry Young, it must be said that
it is amazing to find such an innate and authentic sense of blues tradition in a twenty-year-old musician. At his age, it could hardly have come from personal experience, but it is there nonetheless, to be heard on every track of the album. With guitarist Thornel Schwartz and drummer Jimmy Smith, he forms the Larry Young Trio, so-called on their debut record, Testifying (Prestige/New Jazz 8249). They have worked  together in the Northeast United States, and so have a much more than casual acquaintance with the type of club we are supposedly in at the moment.
And now, the music. The club metaphor is valuable
in many ways, but it would be an insult to the intelli-
gence to go into the old song-and-dance about "this
is a typical set just such as you might hear if you were to walk in ..." It isn't; it was designed for the best possible pacing of a phonograph record, but the tunes themselves, pacing aside, are of that nature and happen to be excellent examples.
Remember is by Irving Berlin, and is of the type
variously called warhorse, old chestnut, or just plain
standard. Of course, it has only achieved that status.
because it is such a good tune, and the easy, rocking
beat of the conga gives it whatever additional 
 freshness is necessary.
Dexter's Deck is by Dexter Gordon, and both the
composer and his composition are veterans of many
more of these clubs than is necessary to qualify.
Jim's Jams is Jimmy Forrest's written contribution
to the session. It is a blues of the type that has come to be known as four-in-the-morning, and the reason is picked for overall quality of mood, this would be it, more than apparent as you listen. If a favorite has to be but that, of course, is a matter of personal taste, and you will have your own.
Bags' Groove aside from having given its name to
one of the greatest jazz sessions of all time (Miles Davis, composer Milt Jackson, and, as the saying goes, "Other of your favorites" on Prestige 7109) has passed into the repertory of classic jazz compositions. That it can be the springboard for improvisations such as these is a good enough reason why.
When Your Lover Has Gone is interpreted by Jimmy
Forrest to reveal the initial anger that must follow the situation expressed in the lyric, rather than the eventual sadness. It is a unique and meaningful interpretation.
Doug Watkins' Help!, previously recorded by Jackie
McLean, is an appropriately happy closer.
It is safe to assume that with the proper company
and refreshment, your own livingroom is your favorite club, and you could do much worse than to book this group.
  --  Notes:  Joe Goldberg

Carlos Salzedo  

     "Scintillation ~ The Harp In High Fidelity" 


IN response to the popular demand which followed the first Mercury recording by Carlos Salzedo of Music for the Harp-MG10144. we take pride in bringing Mr. Salzedo's unique artistry as composer and performing artist to Mercury's CUSTOM FIDELITY series featuring renowned solo artists and chamber ensembles recorded with Mercury's LIVING PRESENCE technique of high fidelity recording.
For nearly a generation, Carlos Salzedo has occupied a unique position with respect to both the musical literature for the harp and its performance; for almost single-handedly he has brought to this instrument more prestige than it has ever before enjoyed this largely by virtue of his own compositions and transcriptions, eight of which are offered on this disc.
Throughout much of the historic past, the harp has functioned chiefly as an instrument to accompany the voice and to enrich the tonal coloration of a large orchestra. However, with the advent of brilliantly original compositions by Carlos Salzedo, such as Scintillation, Whirlwind and the Concerto for Harp and Seven Wind Instruments, the harp has truly come into its own as a virtuoso instrument in much
the same way as the piano after Franz Liszt and the violin after Paganini.
A native of France, Carlos Salzedo has been associated with musical life in America since his 24th year, when he took over the first harp desk of the Metropolitan Opera House Orchestra during Arturo Toscanini's tenure there. Following World War One, Salzedo undertook in earnest his now brilliantly successful mission of reform of methods for performing on the harp, and of interpreting its literature. Not only did he himself compose colorful modern music for the instrument, but he persuaded other leading composers to do likewise. Then, to play this music before the widest possible public, he established the Salzedo Harp Ensemble and joined two of his eminent colleagues in the Barrere-Salzedo-Britt Trio featuring flute, harp and 'cello. Salzedo has even redesigned the harp in its physical aspect along more modern lines; and well over half the harps in use among American symphony orchestras today are the Lyon & Healy "Salzedo Model". Needless to say, Mr. Salzedo's teaching activities have been unceasing from year to year, being centered in New York and Philadelphia during the winter
season and at the famous Salzedo Harp Colony at Camden, Me. during the summer.
  ····   
About the music on this disc ...
"THE HARMONIOUS BLACKSMITH" — AIR WITH VARIATIONS — Handel (arr. Salzedo)-
This is the celebrated set of variations from Handel's Harpsichord Suite No. 5 in E Major from Volume I of the Lessons published at London in 1720. The fanciful title
was not Handel's but the brainchild of some later publisher. The music itself comes from that period of Handel's life which saw the composition of the Water Music, and as such it is broadly melodic and affirmative in its expressive content. The thematic framework is of a simplicity that lends itself ideally to Handel's decorative technique throughout the course of its five variations. Having been written for that queen of plucked keyboard instruments, the harpsichord, it is easy to see why Carlos Salzedo in 1931 should have been attracted to the possibilities of effectively transcribing these Harmonious Blacksmith Variations for the harp medium.
GIGA  —  Corelli (arr. Salzedo) — This charming dance piece ...  Italian violin master, Arcangelo Corelli, is in its original for ...  the A Major Sonata for Violin and Continuo, Op. 5, No. 9, ... among symphony concert audiences in the string orchestra Pinelli. Needless to say, its vital yet elegant rhythmic patterns ... to the harp, for which Mr. Salzedo transcribed the music.
SCINTILLATION  —  Salzedo  —  This is probably the most famous of ... virtuoso compositions for solo harp, abounding as it does with both fascinating effects and colorful musical substance. Written in 1936 following a stay in Mexico, Scintillation is constructed on the basis of idealized dance patterns. The introduction evokes the stately sarabande. There follows a relaxed yet strongly rhythmic rhumba section, then the famous scintillating episode from which this music takes its title. This culminates in a climax of great dynamism and color which takes us back to a shortened recapitulation of the sarabande. A tango-like epilogue prepares the way for the triumphal closing pages.
BALLADE FOR HARP SOLO  —  Salzedo  —  Here is music written by Carlos Salzedo when in his middle twenties-the first of Three Pieces for Solo Harp. In form and expressive content, the music is in the spirit of the romantic piano ballades of Chopin and Liszt. In terms of writing for the harp, Salzedo's Ballade is a virtuoso composition of extraordinary brilliance and difficulty and can well be called a bridge between the older harp style and the modern idiom.
MENUET D'AMOUR -  — Massenet (arr. Salzedo)  —  This plaintive air was in its original form a duet for the two hapless lovers in Massenet's two-act opera of 1907, Thérèse whose action takes place during the French Revolution. The transcription for harp was completed by Mr. Salzedo during 1920. PETITE VALSE  —  Salzedo  —  Another tonal tidbit from The Art of Modulating, and very, Gallic in its 34 manner. Written in 1943, this is the second of a sequence of ten dance pieces, the last eight of which eventually became the Eight Dances recorded by Mr. Salzedo on Mercury MG 10144.  ...
HI-FI FACTS
The wealth of new sonorities devised by Mr. Salzedo for the harp include zylo-harmonic sounds, guitaric sounds, plectric or "brassy" sounds, xylophonic sounds,
tam-tam sounds, timpanic sounds, whistling sounds, eolian flux and many others  —  almost all of which are heard in the course of the music played on this disc. As can well be imagined, Mr. Salzedo's music lends itself especially well to Mercury's LIVING PRESENCE recording technique-and no effort has been spared to achieve the most complete sonic realization of Mr. Salzedo's musical intentions.
The music on this disc was recorded during the summer of 1954 at the studios of Fine Sound, Inc. in New York City. A single Telephone U-47 microphone was used throughout the recording sessions and was hung approximately 8 feet in a perpendicular line from the sounding board of Mr. Salzedo's harp.
ABOUT THE COVER DESIGN for this disc — Bjorn Wiinblad, celebrated young Danish designer of ceramics, textiles and posters, executed a number of specially commissioned cover designs for Mercury recordings late in 1954. A great lover of music himself, especially in recorded form, Wiinblad undertook the work of designing his first covers for long playing records with characteristic eagerness and the results display the fanciful humor and spontaneity so much a part of this distinguished artist's work.
